title: Link an experiment to its data folder
summary: Attach the network folder where an experiment's raw data lives, and open it from the entry in one click.
details: In the Data section of an experiment, paste a network share path (smb://server/share/folder or \\server\share\folder), add an optional label such as "Raw data folder", and press Add.
Each link has buttons to open it on a Mac, to copy the Windows path to paste into Explorer, and to insert a reference to it in the main text.
The label keeps a long path readable. Remove a link with the trash icon while editing.

title: Quick links to LabCollector and your lab's tools
summary: The Links menu in the top bar opens LabCollector and your lab's own pages in one click.
details: Open Links in the top bar to reach LabCollector, OpenIRIS, MoorLab Wiki, ETHIS and MoorLab Zoom. They open in a new tab.
A team admin can change any of these addresses with the pencil icon next to it, so the link always points to the right place.

title: Link templates and see which version you used
summary: Record the template an experiment follows, with or without inserting its content, and keep track of its versions.
details: In an experiment, open Search in the left sidebar and set Type to Experiment templates.
Press Link to associate the template with the experiment without inserting anything, or Add to text to insert its content at the cursor.
Associated templates are listed under Links, each with its version number and how many times it was inserted. Click one to open the template.
Open a template to see its version history and restore an older version; the other versions are kept.

title: Faster scrolling with several spreadsheets
summary: Spreadsheets near the screen now appear as a light preview and become fully editable the moment you click them.
details: Only the table you click gets the full editor, so scrolling past many tables stays smooth.
The preview matches the editor's look, column widths and row heights, so nothing jumps when you click.
The cell you clicked is selected straight away, and the table you are editing stays live while you scroll.
imageAlt: A spreadsheet shown as a light preview with its toolbar; clicking it opens the full editor

highlight.label: Click a table to edit it

title: Tab and Shift+Tab indent several list lines at once
summary: Select multiple bullet or numbered lines and press Tab to indent them all, or Shift+Tab to outdent them.
details: Works for bullet lists, numbered lists and several selected paragraphs.
Nested lists move one level per press.
imageAlt: Several bullet lines selected in the editor; Tab indents them together

title: Version history for templates
summary: See every saved version of a template, compare revisions, and restore an older one without losing the current one.
details: The history opens in a popup on the edit page.
Restoring a version makes it current and keeps the other versions.
Each version has its own edit history that you can restore individually.
imageAlt: The template version history popup listing versions, each with a Restore button and its edit history, outlined

highlight.label: Each version, with Restore and its edit history

title: Insert a spreadsheet of any size, and handier tools in view mode
summary: Drag across a grid to choose the size, like Insert table. View mode now has copy-table and auto-fit buttons.
details: Spreadsheet is also in the classic Insert menu.
Copy the whole table in one click, and auto-fit rows or columns to their content.
Row heights now grow when a narrower column needs more wrapped lines.
imageAlt: The Insert menu with the Spreadsheet size grid and its options, outlined

title: Project management is now Boards, with richer cards
summary: Tasks are now cards, with status badges, deadlines, linked experiments and resources, and bulk actions.
details: Cards show each linked experiment or resource with its status colour.
Select several cards to archive or delete them together.
Steps and comments can be collapsed, and deadlines show how urgent they are.
Duplicate a card into another project, and open a card straight into edit mode.
imageAlt: The Boards page with a card showing its steps and linked experiments, outlined

highlight.label: A card with its steps and linked items

title: Smoother ordering
summary: Attachments can be reused, orders can advance and archive themselves, and notes support lists.
details: Reuse an attachment across orders, and download it with its own button.
Orders can move from requested to ordered when a procurement ID appears, and archive after a set time.
Notes support bulleted and numbered lists, and long titles and file names wrap properly.
imageAlt: The Orders request form with bullet and numbered list buttons above the notes field, outlined

title: More reliable spreadsheet editing
summary: Formulas, fill-drag, undo and cell formatting behave more predictably, in both the inline editor and the popup.
details: Fill-drag keeps absolute references (the ones written with a dollar sign) fixed, so a formula copied down still points at the same cell.
Undo in a spreadsheet only undoes spreadsheet edits, and undo in the text leaves tables alone.
Tab and Enter move between cells, and selected cells and fill-drag are clearly highlighted.
Fixed cell formatting in the popup and a case where saving could blank cells.
imageAlt: A spreadsheet with a selected cell and its fill handle, outlined, under the spreadsheet toolbar

highlight.label: Selected cell with its fill handle

title: A tidier top bar
summary: The navigation bar keeps the key icons visible and folds the rest into a More menu.
details: A Links dropdown groups shortcuts.
The LabCollector link keeps its URL editable from the Tools menu.
imageAlt: The top bar with the More menu open, listing Boards, Orders, Links and Tools

title: Link experiments and resources to your cards
summary: Connect a card to the experiments and resources it is about, and jump between them in one click.
details: Link items while you create a card, or later from the card's detail view.
Use the search panel next to the card to find an experiment or resource, link it, or add it as a step in one move.
Each linked item shows its status colour and type, so you can see at a glance how the work is going.
A project's Linked items section and an All links summary list everything connected to that project, including subprojects.
Click a linked item to open the experiment or resource itself.
imageAlt: A card's detail view with linked experiments and steps, next to the search panel used to link them

title: Better notifications and feedback
summary: You are told when someone gives you access, and the Feedback board can sort by votes or date.
details: Notifications arrive when you gain read access to an experiment or resource, even if you had access before.
The dashboard announcement feed is easier to read.
imageAlt: The notifications dropdown, with a notification that someone gave you access to a resource, outlined

highlight.label: Told when someone shares with you

title: An activity calendar for deadlines and tasks
summary: See every deadline in one calendar: your scheduled tasks together with the unfinished steps of your experiments and resources.
details: Open it from the calendar icon in the left sidebar. A badge counts what is overdue or due within the next hour.
A month grid shows each day's items as small count pills, with clear states for Today, the day you selected, and overdue days. Collapse the grid when you only want the list.
Switch between Day, Week and Month views, and hide weekends if you don't need them. The Today button and 'All visible dates' jump you back or show everything in range.
Below the grid, an agenda lists the items for what you selected, ordered by exact time. Each card says where it came from: a personal task, or a step of an experiment or resource.
Click a step to open its experiment or resource, and mark steps and tasks done right from the agenda, the same way as on the experiment page.
The User and Team switch decides whose experiment and resource steps you see.
Give a task a title, notes, an exact date and time, and a reminder: at the deadline, 15 minutes, 1 hour, 1 day or 1 week before, or a custom number of minutes.
Reminders appear as one grouped, collapsible banner that stays as you move between pages, and they also arrive as notifications and email, following your existing step-deadline preference.
Subscribe to your deadlines from Google Calendar or Apple Calendar with a private link from the Calendar tab. The link is read-only, and you can regenerate or revoke it at any time.
imageAlt: The activity calendar panel in the left sidebar: month grid, Day/Week/Month buttons and legend, outlined

title: A left sidebar with your tools one click away
summary: A slim rail on the left keeps folders, search, to-dos and the calendar open next to your work, on every page.
details: Folders: browse and manage your experiment folders, pin a favorite, and collapse branches you don't need.
Search: your saved filters and results, combined in one place.
Quick search and commands: press Ctrl/Cmd + K from anywhere.
To-do list: tasks and step deadlines sorted by due date, with a count of what is due.
Activity calendar: a Day, Week or Month view of deadlines, with your external calendar.
On experiment pages a table of contents tab lists the headings so you can jump around, and filter sections to print or copy.
The rail stays put while you scroll, and the last panel you opened is remembered.
imageAlt: The left sidebar: the rail of tabs (folders, search, quick search, to-do, calendar) next to an open panel, rail outlined

title: Folders and READMEs
summary: A shared tree of folders for experiments and resources, each with its own README and permissions.
details: Open the Folders tab in the left sidebar. The tree shows every folder; the number next to a folder counts the items inside it.
Press Create folder at the bottom, give it a name (and an optional short description) and choose a parent folder to nest it.

A good way to use them: one folder for each project, and a subfolder inside it for each idea within that project that you want to test and verify. Each approach then has its own place, and you can compare them side by side.
Click a folder to list only what is inside it. Choose the folder when you create an experiment or resource, or change it on its edit page.
Press the three dots on a folder for Export, Edit (rename, move to another parent, change the description) and Delete. Deleting a folder moves its items to Unfiled.
Press the page icon on a folder to open its README: a page of notes for everyone working in that folder. The folder's owner and admins edit it; everyone who can see the folder can read it.
Star a folder to bookmark it, and collapse the branches you do not need. The tree remembers what you opened.
Set who can see and edit a folder's contents: open the three dots, press Edit, then Permissions (shown to the folder's owner and admins).

Choose who can see and who can edit with the same options as on a single experiment: a base level, plus teams, user groups or specific people. Leave Include subfolders ticked to cover the whole tree, check the item count the dialog shows, and press Apply.

The permissions of every item you can edit are replaced (items that are not yours, locked or archived are skipped and counted). The folder remembers the choice, so items created in it, moved into it or filed in a new subfolder take the same permissions.
You can still change one experiment on its own afterwards. It stays as you set it until the next Apply on that folder.
purpose: Keep the lab organised in folders the whole team sees, and decide once who can see and edit everything in a folder.
uses: One folder per project, with a README that lists the project protocols and naming rules.
Inside a project, one subfolder per idea you want to test and verify, so each approach keeps its own experiments and you can compare the results.
Export a whole folder (PDF or ZIP) when a paper is submitted or a person leaves.
Give a project folder read access to the whole team but edit access only to the project members, in one step.
Keep a private folder for drafts that only you and a few colleagues can open.
news: Folders now hold resources as well as experiments, can be bookmarked, have READMEs, can be exported, and can remember permissions that apply to everything inside.
shot: The Folders tab with a project folder open and its README beside it, and the Folder permissions dialog with the Can see tab open

title: Quick search and commands
summary: Press Ctrl + K (Cmd + K on a Mac) on any page to find an experiment, resource, folder or heading, or to run a command, from the keyboard.
details: Open it with Ctrl + K (Cmd + K on a Mac) on any page, even while you are typing in the editor, or with the lightning bolt button on the left edge. Press Escape or click outside the window to close it.

With the box empty it lists commands. On an edit page these include Save, Save and go back, Insert date, Insert title, Insert note, Insert table or spreadsheet and Insert link. On every page: Open folders, Open filters, Search everything, Open tasks, Open calendar and Open table of contents.
Start typing to narrow the list. It matches the name of a command and the words that describe it.
It also finds headings in the entry you are looking at (choosing one scrolls to it) and the folders in your folder tree (choosing one opens it).

After two letters it searches your experiments and resources by title and lists the matches, with their category. Choosing one opens it. If you have unsaved changes while editing, it asks before leaving.
Move through the list with the up and down arrow keys and press Enter to choose, or click a result. Up to 24 results are shown.
purpose: Get anywhere, or do something, without taking your hands off the keyboard or hunting through menus.
uses: Press Ctrl + K, type a few letters of an old experiment's title and open it.
While writing, press Ctrl + K and choose Insert date, or Save, without reaching for the toolbar.
Jump to a heading in a long experiment by typing part of it.
Open the To-do list or the calendar from the keyboard.
news: New: a keyboard-first quick search and command window, available on every page.
shot: The quick search window open over a page, with a few letters typed and experiment and command results listed

title: Activity calendar
summary: One calendar for what is coming and what you have already done: your tasks plus the unfinished steps of your experiments.
details: Open it from the calendar icon in the left sidebar. A badge counts what is overdue or due within the next hour.
A month grid shows each day with small count pills, and marks today, the day you selected and overdue days. Switch between Day, Week and Month views, and hide weekends if you do not need them.
Below the grid, an agenda lists the items for what you selected, in time order. Each card says where it came from: a personal task, or a step of an experiment or resource.

Click a step to open its experiment, and tick steps and tasks off right from the agenda. A completed task stays on its day with the time you finished it, so you can look back at what was done and when.
Add a task with a title, notes, an exact date and time and a reminder (at the deadline, or 15 minutes, 1 hour, 1 day or 1 week before).
Subscribe from Google Calendar or Apple Calendar with the private, read-only link on the Calendar tab. You can regenerate or revoke it any time.
purpose: See what is due this week at a glance, never miss a step deadline hidden inside an experiment, and look back at what you finished on earlier days.
uses: Plan the week on Monday: switch to Week view and see every deadline across your experiments.
Go back to a past week or month to see which tasks you completed and when, for a weekly report or a lab meeting update.
Put the subscription link in your phone calendar so lab deadlines show up next to the rest of your day.
news: New: an activity calendar that combines tasks and experiment steps, with reminders and calendar subscriptions.
shot: The Activity calendar panel with the month grid, the Day/Week/Month buttons and the agenda below

title: Project Boards
summary: Plan lab work as projects of cards, with deadlines and steps, and link each card to its experiments and resources.
details: Open Boards from the top bar (under More). Create a project, then add cards for the tasks in it.
A card has a title, notes, a deadline, steps, comments and people assigned to it. Status badges and deadline colours show at a glance what needs attention.
Steps and comments can be collapsed to keep a long card short.
Select several cards to archive or delete them together. Duplicate a card into another project, or open a card straight into edit mode.
Projects can hold subprojects, be pinned to stay on top, and be archived when finished.
To tie a card to the work it is about, open the search panel next to the card while you create it, or later from its detail view.

Find an experiment or resource, then press Link, or add it as a step in one move. Each linked item shows its type icon and a coloured dot for its status, on the card as well as in the project, so you can see how the work is going.
A project's Linked items section and the All links summary list everything connected to that project, including subprojects. Click a linked item to open the experiment or resource itself.
purpose: Keep track of who does what and by when in one board per project, with the plan and the experiments pointing at each other.
uses: One board per paper or grant, with a card for each experiment series and each deadline.
A board for lab chores, with a card per task and the person responsible.
Link the protocol template and the experiment for each planned run, and open the project to see which linked experiments are finished.
news: Boards replace the old project list, with richer cards, bulk actions, subprojects, and cards that link to experiments and resources with their status colours.
shot: The Boards page with a project open and one card showing its steps and linked experiments, and the search panel used to link them

title: Orders
summary: Track things to order for the team, from request to delivery.
details: Open Orders from the top bar (under More) and press New order. Say what you need, with the supplier and any link or catalogue number.
Add the supplier details and notes (lists are supported), and attach quotes or invoices. An attachment can be reused on other orders.

Statuses: an order is Requested (asked for), Ordered (placed with the supplier), Received (it has arrived), Backlogged (known to be needed but not requested yet) or Cancelled. Change it with the coloured dropdown at the top of the order.
Tabs: All, Requested, Ordered, Received, Backlogged and Cancelled show one status at a time. All shows everything that is not archived. Archived holds the orders you have archived.
To change several orders at once, tick them and use Move to status… in the bar that appears.
Ordered and Received orders show a Missing Procurement ID warning when no procurement ID was found in an attached file.
The person who placed an order is notified when someone else changes its status.
Pin an order by hand to keep it at the top of the list, on every tab, until you unpin it.

Pinned for all and Reference are two special kinds of order with no status and no dropdown. Pinned for all is shared with the team and stays at the top for everyone. Reference is only for you: nobody else sees it, and it stays at the top of the All tab for you. Each has its own tab and does not show on the status tabs.

Tick Pinned for all or Reference when you create an order, or later when you edit it. Once an order is one of them it cannot go back to Requested, Ordered or another status. You can switch it between the two in the edit form (the author or a team admin; only the author can make an order a Reference).
You can set a reminder on an order.

Templates: the Templates tab on the Orders page holds texts that go with ordering, such as an email to a supplier or a quote request. Everyone in the team can search them and copy the text; the author or a team admin edits them.
purpose: One place to request what the lab needs and to see where each order is, instead of emails and sticky notes.
uses: Request a reagent, attach the supplier quote and let the person who orders pick it up.
Mark an order Received when it arrives, so the list always shows what is still on its way.
Keep a supplier's catalogue number or standing order details as a Reference of your own, or as Pinned for all for the whole team.
Keep a standard quote-request email as a template, copy it, fill in the supplier and the product, and send it from your mail program.
news: New: reusable attachments, reminders, notes with lists, the Pinned for all and Reference kinds, and shared text templates for supplier emails.
shot: The Orders page with a few orders at different stages and one order open

title: Link items to experiments
summary: Connect an experiment to the resources, data folders, templates and tools it uses, and reach the lab's tools in one click.
details: Scroll below the main text. Each section opens and closes on its own.
Steps and tasks: a checklist for the experiment, with deadlines that also show in your calendar.

Data: link the network folder where the experiment’s raw data lives. Paste the path (smb://server/share/folder or \\server\share\folder), add an optional label such as “Raw data folder” and press Add.
Each data link has buttons to open it on a Mac, to copy the Windows path to paste into Explorer, and to insert a reference to it in the main text. Remove a link with the trash icon while editing.
Links: other experiments, associated templates, resources, orders, web addresses and LabCollector entries this one relates to.
Files / folders and Local files: attach files, or paste references to files kept elsewhere.
Compounds and Custom fields: record chemicals from the compound database, and any extra fields your team defined.
The Links menu in the top bar opens LabCollector, OpenIRIS, the MoorLab Wiki, ETHIS and MoorLab Zoom in a new tab, from any page.

A team admin can change any of these addresses with the pencil icon next to it, so the link always points to the right place. On an experiment, the LabCollector links section lists the LabCollector entries it relates to.
purpose: Record not only what you did but also what you used, where the data lives, what it relates to, and reach the tools the lab uses without bookmarks.
uses: Link the resources you refer to, such as the record of the meeting where the experiment was planned, so anyone can follow the trail.
Add a step with a deadline for the next measurement and see it in the calendar.
Link the folder with the microscope images or the sequencing run, and insert the reference where you describe the measurement.
Jump to the lab wiki for a protocol while you write an experiment, or join the group meeting with the Zoom link.
news: New: the Data section for network folders, order, template and LabCollector links in these sections, and a Links menu that folds the lab’s tools into the top bar.
shot: An experiment page scrolled to the sections under the main text with the Data section open, and the top bar with the Links menu open

title: Templates and their versions
summary: Link a template to an experiment, see which version you used, and restore older versions.
details: In an experiment, open Search in the left sidebar and set Type to Experiment templates.
Press Link to record the template without inserting anything, or Add to text to insert its content at the cursor.
Associated templates are listed under Links with their version number and how many times they were inserted. Click one to open it.
Open a template to see its version history, compare versions and restore an older one. The other versions are kept.
Star the templates you use most to find them quickly.
purpose: Start from the lab’s standard protocol and know exactly which version of it an experiment followed.
uses: Keep the standard protocol as a template and publish a new version when it changes.
Months later, see which experiments used the old version.
news: New: template versions, version history with restore, and template links on experiments.
shot: The template version history with the list of versions and the Restore buttons

title: Feedback board and announcements
summary: Post ideas and bugs, upvote the ones that matter, and read team announcements.
details: Open Feedback from the top bar. Post a bug or feature idea for your team and upvote the ones that matter most to you.
Sort the list by votes or by date.
The dashboard shows the announcement feed: pinned announcements stay on top, and you can react to them.
You are notified when someone mentions you in feedback.
purpose: Tell the people who run the system what would help, and see what the team cares about most.
uses: Ask for a new field or a new link, and see how many colleagues want it too.
Read the latest lab news at the top of the dashboard.
news: New: a feedback board with votes and an announcement feed on the dashboard.
shot: The Feedback board sorted by votes, next to the dashboard announcement feed

title: Search, favourite filters and linking
summary: Search with your favourite filters, then attach what you find to an experiment or paste a link to it, without leaving the page.
details: Open the Search tab in the left sidebar. Pick a Type (All, Experiments, Resources, Experiment templates or Resource templates) and type in the search box.
The Filters list shows your favourite categories, tags, statuses and owners for that type. Tick the ones you want and press Apply filters.
Press Manage to choose which ones are your favourites. They are saved only for your account.
Results appear below, with a link to the full list.

Attach while editing: open an experiment or resource in edit mode, search in the panel, and press the link button on a result to attach that experiment or resource to the one you are editing. It then shows under Links.
Paste a link: press the second button on a result to put a link to it into the text, at the cursor.
For templates, the link button records the template an experiment came from, and the second button inserts the template's content at the cursor instead of a link.
With a board card open, results also get a button to link them to that card, and one to add them as a step on it.
purpose: Stop re-entering the same filters every time you look for something, and link what you find into your work in one click.
uses: Favourite your own tags and the statuses you use, then filter “my running experiments” in two clicks.
Switch Type to Resources to look through meeting records and other resources with the same panel.
While writing up an experiment, search for its protocol template and press the link button to record it, then paste a link to the earlier experiment next to the sentence that refers to it.
Search a template while editing and insert its content straight into the experiment.
news: New: filters you can favourite, shared by search across experiments, resources and templates, plus attach and paste-a-link buttons on every result.
shot: The Search panel next to an experiment being edited, with the attach and paste-a-link buttons on a result outlined

title: Table of contents in experiments
summary: A list of the headings of an experiment so you can jump around, show only the sections you pick, and print or copy only parts of it.
details: On an experiment page, open the Table of Contents tab in the left sidebar.
The Document sections list shows the headings. Click one to jump to it.
Use Add filter or Add heading filter to select sections, and choose whether all or any of the filters must match.
To read only some parts, open Select headings to filter or print and tick the headings you want. The experiment then shows just those sections and hides the rest, until you clear the selection.
Press Print selection or Copy filtered content to get only those parts. Switch spreadsheets and pictures on or off.
purpose: Long experiments become easy to move through, and you can share just the part someone needs.
uses: Copy just the Methods part of an experiment into an email.
Print the results sections of a long experiment for a meeting.
Tick only the Results headings to read them without scrolling past the methods.
news: New: a contents tab with section filters, print and copy.
shot: An experiment with the Table of Contents panel open and a few headings selected

title: Notifications
summary: A bell that tells you what needs you, so you do not have to check every page.
details: The bell in the top bar collects your notifications and shows how many are new.
You are notified when someone gives you access to an experiment or resource, mentions you in a comment, assigns you a task or a card, or changes the status of an order.
Step deadlines can also arrive by email, following your existing preference.
purpose: Be told when something changes for you, without checking every page.
uses: Share an experiment and the person you shared it with gets a notification right away.
Mention a colleague with @name in a card comment and they are notified.
news: New: notifications for assignments, mentions and access.
shot: The notifications dropdown open from the bell in the top bar

title: The editor toolbar
summary: New buttons above the text of an experiment: one Insert menu, dates, titles, notes, checklists, spreadsheets, links and more.
details: Save: the first button saves the experiment, and the bar shows whether your changes are saved. Save and go back is in the File menu.
Insert: one menu for everything you can add. It lists what you used recently, then Text (title, date, notes, divider), Tables, Links and Laboratory (templates).
Checklist: turns lines into tick boxes. Type [ ] and a space to start one, then click a box to tick it.

Format painter and Clear formatting: at the end of the toolbar, next to the special characters, emoji and code buttons. Copy the look of some text and apply it to other text, or strip formatting from the selection.
Links: add a web link, upload and link a file or folder, refer to a file or folder on a shared drive, or link a LabCollector item.
Day: inserts today's date in your saved format. The arrow gives Custom date, Log entry (date and time), and Edit, Copy link and Delete for a date you selected. Double-click a date to edit it.
Title: puts the experiment title in as a heading. The arrow lets you pick the title style and save it as your default.
Divider: single or double, solid or dashed lines to separate parts of your notes.
Note: inserts a highlighted note box. The arrow sets the title, whether it appears in the table of contents, and the heading level.

Table, spreadsheet and well plate: one menu to insert a table, a formula spreadsheet or a 6 to 384 well plate, edit or autofit the selected spreadsheet, style tables and cells, indent tables and make them sortable.
Copy table: copies a whole table or your selection with its formatting, ready to paste into another program.
Template: search your templates and insert one into the experiment. Favourites come first.
Keyboard shortcuts: Ctrl+Shift+D date and time, Ctrl+Alt+T title, Ctrl+Alt+N note, Ctrl+Shift+H single line, Ctrl+Alt+Shift+H double line.
On a long experiment the toolbar stays at the top as you scroll and slides smoothly with the top bar.
The “i” at the very end of the toolbar opens this guide card.
purpose: Find every editing tool in one place, and write and structure an experiment faster with fewer clicks.
uses: Press Insert, then Text, then Log entry each time you return to an experiment so that your notes read as a dated record.
Start a protocol step list with a checklist, then tick the boxes off at the bench.
Insert a note box with a clear title for a warning or a deviation so that it shows up in the table of contents.
news: New: one Insert menu, checklists, a format painter, date, title and note tools with saved defaults, spreadsheets and well plates, and a template picker.
shot: The editor toolbar of an experiment with the Insert menu open

title: Working together: members, assignments and comments
summary: Add colleagues to a project, assign cards to people, and talk about the work in comments where you can @mention anyone.
details: Open a project's edit dialog and use Team members on this project to add colleagues. Remove someone with the × on their name.
A subproject starts with the same members as its parent. Members of a parent project can already see and manage its subprojects, and you can still add more people to a subproject.
Open a card and choose people under Assigned to. You can assign several people, and remove one with the ×. Left empty, the card is assigned to you.
Each assigned person gets a notification, and the card shows who created it and who it was assigned by. Use Assigned to me above the board to see just your cards.
Cards assigned to you also appear in the To-do tab in the left sidebar.
Comments: every card has a Comments section. Write a comment, and type @ followed by a name to mention someone. The person you mention is notified.
The same comments with @mentions work on tasks in the To-do list and on posts in the Feedback board. You can edit or delete your own comments.
Cards show a comment count, so you can see which ones have a discussion going without opening them.
purpose: Make clear who is on a project, who is responsible for each card, and keep the discussion next to the work instead of in emails.
uses: Add the whole project team once, then assign a card to the person who will run each experiment.
Ask a question on a card with @name, so the person gets a notification and the answer stays with the card.
Create a subproject for one paper figure and let it start with the same people as the main project.
news: New: project members, several people per card, comments with @mentions, and notifications when you are assigned or mentioned.
shot: A card open with the Assigned to field and the Comments section showing an @mention

title: To-do list
summary: Your tasks and the deadlines of your experiment steps in one list: add, remind, tick off, look back, and subscribe from your own calendar.
details: Open the To-do list from the checklist button in the left sidebar. The red number on the button counts what is overdue or due soon. The refresh button reloads the list.
The panel has two tabs. Tasks is the list; Calendar shows a month and the tasks of the day you pick.
The Tasks list is grouped by due date: Overdue, Today, Tomorrow, then each later day, and No due date at the end. It mixes your own tasks with the steps of your experiments that have a deadline.
A step shows the name of its experiment, and an Add a deadline link when it has no deadline yet. Click the step to open the experiment. Ticking it marks the step complete in the experiment.
Add a task: type it in the box at the top and press Enter or the plus button. Press the arrow beside the box for more: notes, the board project it belongs to, a date and a time, and a reminder.
Reminders: at the deadline, or 15 minutes, 1 hour, 1 day or 1 week before, or after a number of minutes you choose, or at a specific date and time. A reminder needs a date and time first.
Each row has a handle to drag it into a new order or onto another day, a button to edit it, and Done to tick it off. Click the task's title to open its details.
In a task's details you can add a description and notes (bold, italic, headings, bullet and numbered lists, links), link items, add steps and write comments.

Linked items: press Open Search to link and use the link buttons on the results to attach experiments, resources and templates. You can also add a web address or a network folder (smb://) with a label. On a Mac the network folder opens directly; on Windows you can copy its path to paste into Explorer.
Steps: break a task into smaller steps and tick them off one by one. Comments: write a note to your colleagues and type @ followed by a name to mention someone, who is then notified.
At the bottom of the details: Archive (puts the task away), Duplicate (a copy to adjust), Delete (asks first and cannot be undone), and Edit.
Done tasks move to Completed tasks below the list. Choose how far back to look, from the past day to the past month, and press Restore to bring one back.
Archived tasks, also below the list, holds the tasks you archived. Open it to see them and press Unarchive to bring one back.
The Calendar tab shows a month. Pick a day to see its tasks and the tasks you completed on it, and move between months with the arrows.

Subscribe from your own calendar: on the Calendar tab press Create private link, then add it to Google Calendar or Apple Calendar. The link is read-only and shows your task titles and deadlines, so keep it private. You can regenerate or revoke it at any time. Google Calendar needs the link to be reachable from the internet.
Board cards assigned to you appear in this list as well. The Project boards button above the list opens the boards. When someone assigns you a task, you get a notification from the bell.
purpose: Know what is due today and never lose a step deadline inside an experiment.
uses: Start the day by opening the list and ticking off what is done.
Add a task with a reminder the moment you think of it, such as ordering a reagent by Friday.
Keep the list open on a busy day and tick off steps as you finish them.
Link the experiment and the network folder with the raw data to a task, so everything for it is one click away.
On Friday, open Completed tasks for the past week to see what you finished, for a report or a meeting.
Put the private calendar link in your phone's calendar so your deadlines appear next to the rest of your day.
news: New: one list for tasks and step deadlines with reminders, steps and comments on tasks, linked items, a completed and archived history, a calendar view, and a calendar subscription.
